proposal: T1 - Evergreen Redwood T2 - Yew We wish to remove a large evergreen redwood which is just 2.5m from our house and is causing concern with regard to our kitchen foundations. In addition it casts a long and deep shadow over our family outside seating area and our kitchen. Immediately behind the redwood is a mature Yew tree which impairs the canopy of the redwood making it partially misshapen. Together, the 2 canopies present a very dark and dull appearance, very close to the house. The Redwood appears healthy, however, we would like to replace it with several less sombre trees having brighter foliage and canopies that allow more light to penetrate onto the ground and into the windows of our kitchen. I propose one Liquidambar Styraciflua Worplesdon and beyond it a Tibetan Cherry and an Amelanchier lamarchkii (service berry). If there is room I would like to also plant a Liriodendron Tuliifera Aureomarginatum to give contrast and colour. These trees would, I feel, mix well with others already there including a box tree and a Betula utilis Jacquemontii. As part of a small scheme in the area of the redwood, we intend to plant a hedge line using a mix of beech & some hazel in front of a fence which leads to a garden shed and which extends for approx 40 metres. In addition we are proposing to plant several trees along the exterior of the fence which is within our boundary and is adjacent to Ferry Lane. These trees are intended to enhance the tree line, act as a deterrent to intruders and screen both the fence and some unsightly tall stumps in the neighbouring property, Ferry Lodge. I propose planting 3 Cercis Canadensis (Forest Pansy), 3 Ligustrum Lucidum Variegata, interspersed with 2 or 3 Turkish Hazel - Corylus Colurna. We will also plant some hedgerow behind the trees. In addition to the above, we want to reduce the canopy of several mature Yew trees, to allow more light and to encourage growth of the trees in front of them.We would also like to remove a Yew tree adj to the garden shed. To remove a weak, thin yew which, again, inhibits the planting of replacement trees and appears both weak and very unsightly. Trimming, we fear, would probably not prove helpful, even in the long term and it is in a perfect position, in the centre of the bed, for a replacement young tree. 3. To remove a spindly spruce pine which is weak in habit and form and is masked by yews and will not benefit from trimming as it does not have any healthy low branches. proposal: T1 - Yew tree We have consulted a tree surgeon who stated that whilst it is hard to estimate the age of yew trees in particular, without the photographic evidence he suggested 100-200 years. The photographic evidence clearly narrows that date range. We may therefore conclude that the yew tree currently growing beside the 1792 tomb probably dates from around 1900 (midway between 1880 and 1900). Opinion of Tree Surgeon regarding safety However, although the tree appears at first glance to be a single stem, the surgeon advised that the tree is not a single stem but a co-dominant stem, creating a point of weakness where the two stems diverge. He further advised that if the church-side stem were to fall for any reason it would do so towards the church, with a potential for major damage to the chancel and the lady chapel, including the Kempe windows. Given that: a) the 1792 tomb tree is almost certainly no older than 100 years; b) it causes repeated damage to the grade II* listed church in that, despite pruning, it sheds dead leaves into the valley between the chancel and lady chapel roofs, creating leaks that have repeatedly soaked the roof timbers and internal wall of the lady chapel; c) it blocks the light from the two CE Kempe east windows of the church, thereby substantially reducing their visual impact and detracting from the Kempe's work and from the overall aesthetic value of the grade II* church; d) it is jeopardising the continued existence of the grade II listed 1792 tomb; e) if the tree were to fail at its point of weakness, there is potential for major damage to the grade II* listed church. Permission is therefore requested to fell the said yew tree and treat the stump so as to prevent any regrowth. The church would be prepared to plant a replacement tree elsewhere in the churchyard.
